correctness.rationale: Necessity follows because two initially white open twins always have the same white-neighbor count at every stage and therefore neither can be the unique white neighbor of a forcing vertex. For sufficiency, order the canonical chain-graph twin classes by nested neighborhoods. If white vertices remain and every class contains at most one white vertex, choose an extremal white class on one side; the strict nesting created by absence of a second white twin produces a vertex in the adjacent difference whose unique white neighbor is that extremal vertex. Iterating removes all white vertices. The product enumerator then follows independently in each twin class. A fresh exhaustive replay over 253 canonical connected chain-graph profiles with one to three levels, class sizes one to three and at most ten vertices checked 150,292 subsets and found no disagreement with the criterion.
risks: The statement assumes the standard connected chain-graph canonical decomposition; isolated-vertex variants would require separate bookkeeping.

final_claim: For every finite connected chain graph, a set is skew zero forcing exactly when it omits at most one vertex from each open-neighborhood twin class. Consequently its skew-zero-forcing polynomial is the product over twin classes \(T\) of \(x^{|T|}+|T|x^{|T|-1}\), so \(Z^-(G)=|V(G)|-|\mathcal T|\) and the number of minimum sets is \(\prod_{T\in\mathcal T}|T|\).
limitations: Finite connected chain graphs under the standard skew color-change rule only.
